questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery incidence in a service survey
questions.learningObjective: State what a service survey incidence figure measures
questions.stem: A field biologist surveying rural clinics asks households whether they paid an unofficial fee to obtain a birth certificate in the past year.

options.text: The share of households reporting a payment, a measure of reported experience rather than a count of cases
The total number of bribes paid in the district during the year, which the survey counts directly
options.misconception: treats a survey share as a direct event count

options.text: The share of clinic staff who demand payment, which the survey can identify from households
options.misconception: confuses household reports with staff behaviour

options.text: The difference in fees between clinics that were visited and those that were not
options.misconception: reads the survey design as a fee comparison

questions.explanation: A service survey asks users whether they encountered a payment, so its incidence is the proportion reporting one, not a count of all bribes. It captures reported experience of a named service and period.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey actually counted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Three forms of corruption
questions.learningObjective: Classify recorded cases into bribery, theft of public funds and procurement fraud
questions.stem: The survey classifies 150 recorded cases: 78 as bribery, 44 as theft of public funds, and 28 as fraud in procurement.

options.text: The bribery share is the largest single group, so bribery is the only form the district faces
options.misconception: treats the largest group as the only group

options.text: The three categories divide recorded cases by mechanism, with bribery the largest at just over half
The theft cases should be counted as bribery because money left public hands in both
options.misconception: merges distinct mechanisms into one form

options.text: The procurement fraud cases overlap with bribery, so the total case count cannot be trusted
options.misconception: assumes overlap without any evidence of it

questions.explanation: The three forms are bribery, theft of public funds and fraud in procurement, distinguished by how the money is obtained. Here bribery leads at 78 of 150, but all three mechanisms are present in the survey population.
questions.hint: Ask what mechanism each category describes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Explain why unofficial fees impose a cost on the public purse
questions.stem: The survey finds that unofficial fees at a district clinic are paid from household budgets, while the clinic keeps the payments and pays nothing to the health budget.

options.text: The public purse is unaffected, because the money moves between private households and private clinics
options.misconception: ignores the link between private fees and public services

options.text: The public purse is unaffected, because clinic staff add the fee to their own pay rather than diverting funds
options.misconception: assumes staff pay is the only way fees are lost

options.text: The public purse bears a cost, because households pay for the same service twice, once in fees and once in taxes
The public purse benefits, because the fees are collected locally and stay within the district
options.misconception: treats local collection as a public gain

questions.explanation: A household that pays an unofficial fee and also finances the clinic through taxes has funded the service twice. The fee is not a neutral transfer between private parties because the service being paid for is publicly provided.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same service is being paid for twice.

questions.topic: Bribery as a cost of doing business
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total value of unofficial payments recorded in the survey
questions.stem: Informants across the survey area recorded 45 unofficial payments of 60 units each for access to public services. What is the combined value of those payments?
questions.explanation: Forty-five payments at 60 units each give 45 times 60, which is 2,700. For the surveyed businesses this is a cost of doing business, a predictable charge that raises the price of every licence.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Rent-seeking through a licence
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a discretionary licence creates rent-seeking
questions.stem: The biologist's report must explain to district officials why a licence regime produces rent-seeking rather than simply raising revenue.

options.text: Because licences are issued by officials who may also be bidders for the same opportunities
options.misconception: assumes officials bid for licences

options.text: Because a licence sets a price that firms would have paid anyway, so the fee is really a tax
options.misconception: redefines rent-seeking as ordinary taxation

options.text: Because the licence takes so long to issue that firms hire agents to do nothing but wait
options.misconception: reduces rent-seeking to administrative delay

options.text: Because a licence is a scarce permission that officials can grant selectively, creating a prize worth paying for

questions.explanation: Rent-seeking arises when a permission is scarce and allocated discretionarily, so the holder can capture a prize by securing it faster than rivals. The fee then behaves like a price for privileged access.
questions.hint: Ask what the licence holder gains from the licence's scarcity.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A licensing queue before and after reform
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a licence queue reform using its median and its longest waits

stimulus.body: We timed 120 licence applications at the district office. Before the reform, the median wait was 240 days and the longest wait was 611. After the reform, the median wait was 75 days and the longest was 190. The published target for the reformed process is 60 days at the median. A minority of applicants told us they had offered a personal payment in order to be served sooner, and the share who said so was higher among those who waited longest.

questions.stem: The survey quotes a business note on the licensing queue; the note is reproduced below.

options.text: The reform shortened the typical wait substantially, but a long tail remains and the slowest cases are where payments concentrate
The reform solved the queue, since every application is now inside the published sixty-day target
options.misconception: treats a median as if it were the maximum

options.text: The queue is unchanged, since the longest waits before and after the reform are broadly comparable
options.misconception: compares only the tail and ignores the typical case

options.text: The shorter waits show that payments were never part of the queue, only of the formal process
options.misconception: separates the queue from the informal fee without evidence

questions.explanation: The median fell from 240 to 75 days, but the target is 60 and the longest waits stay near 190. Payment accounts cluster among the slowest cases. A single median would hide that.
questions.hint: Look at the spread behind the median.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tenure and the defence of office
questions.learningObjective: Explain how tenure changes the private cost of leaving office
questions.stem: A district reform team asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, how long tenure changes the balance between defending office and serving the public.

answer.exemplar: An official who holds office on a protected tenure faces very little cost from leaving it, because dismissal would trigger a legal claim or an expensive dispute, and because the office itself carries a perquisite. An official on a short or probationary term can be replaced at low cost, so the cost of resisting a superior's instruction falls on that official rather than on the public. Where tenure is strong, posts tend to be defended even when the person holding them has become poorly suited to the post, and where it is weak, good staff may leave at the first sign that the post can be taken from them.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate links tenure to the private cost of leaving office and then to staff behaviour. A strong answer explains the incentive in each direction, not merely a verdict on tenure.
questions.hint: Ask what it costs an official to lose the post.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Nepotism in appointment
questions.learningObjective: Identify nepotism as allocation by family connection rather than by open competition
questions.stem: The survey finds that 31 of 45 senior appointments went to relatives of serving officers.

options.text: This is ordinary recruitment because relatives of officers are likely to be better trained than others
options.misconception: assumes family connection improves competence

options.text: This is nepotism, since appointment by family connection bypasses the open competition the process claims to use
This is not nepotism, because no rule has yet been broken in any individual appointment
options.misconception: requires a proven breach before naming nepotism

options.text: This shows the region has a small pool of candidates, since qualified applicants are always scarce
options.misconception: explains family hiring by candidate scarcity

questions.explanation: Nepotism is the use of family connection to secure appointment, whether or not any single case can be shown unlawful. A pattern in which most posts go to relatives bypasses open competition.
questions.hint: Ask how the posts were won rather than who won.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery incidence in a service survey
questions.learningObjective: Compare reported incidence across services using a common denominator
questions.stem: A survey of 320 households found 74 reported an unofficial fee at a clinic, 51 at a school office and 29 at a water point.

options.text: The clinic figure is the lowest incidence, since 74 out of 320 is a smaller share than the rest
options.misconception: misreads a raw count as the lowest rate

options.text: The water point figure is the highest incidence, since 29 out of 320 exceeds the other two
options.misconception: compares counts as if the largest were the highest rate

options.text: The clinic has the highest reported incidence at about 23 per cent, and the water point the lowest at 9 per cent
The three figures cannot be compared, since each service was reached by a different number of households
options.misconception: assumes unstated denominators invalidate comparison

questions.explanation: 74 of 320 is about 23 per cent, 51 of 320 about 16 and 29 of 320 about 9. With the same denominator, the clinic stands out as the service where reported payment is most frequent.
questions.hint: Put each count over the same denominator.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Three forms of corruption
questions.learningObjective: Separate bribery, theft and fraud by the mechanism each involves
questions.stem: In the survey a clinic clerk collects a small sum for a service the household was entitled to receive free, and a procurement officer inflates the price of a bulk medicine order.

options.text: Both cases are the same form, since in each the public is paying more than it should
options.misconception: groups cases by shared outcome rather than mechanism

options.text: Both cases are fraud, since each involves a public official misrepresenting the rules
options.misconception: treats any misrepresentation as fraud

options.text: The first case is fraud and the second is bribery, because fraud requires a higher value
options.misconception: distinguishes forms by amount rather than mechanism

options.text: The first is bribery and the second is fraud, because one is payment for a service and the other a falsified invoice

questions.explanation: The forms are separated by mechanism: bribery pays to secure a service, theft takes public funds, and fraud deceives through a falsified invoice or inflated price. The two cases use different mechanisms.
questions.hint: Ask how the money was obtained in each case.

questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a public appropriation lost to intermediaries
questions.stem: The survey estimates that 8 per cent of the district's 2,500,000 unit health budget leaks to intermediaries each year. What value does that represent?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery as a cost of doing business
questions.learningObjective: Argue that unofficial payments belong in an analysis of commercial costs
questions.stem: The survey report must explain to the district's business association why unofficial payments belong in an analysis of commercial costs.

options.text: Because they are a predictable charge on turnover that firms pass on, like any other input cost
Because they are a tax that the association should campaign to reduce rather than to count
options.misconception: treats unofficial payments as ordinary taxation

options.text: Because they only matter for firms that operate formally, so the informal ones need no analysis
options.misconception: assumes informal firms are unaffected by fees

options.text: Because they show that the district's market is competitive enough to attract so much demand
options.misconception: reads widespread payments as evidence of competition

questions.explanation: A payment required to obtain a licence or permit behaves like a cost of production, raising prices and discouraging entry. Treating it as a tax misses that firms change prices because of it.
questions.hint: Ask how a firm treats the payment in its pricing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Rent-seeking through a licence
questions.learningObjective: Recognise rent-seeking in the contrast between an ordinary queue and a paid fast route

stimulus.body: Our members report that the district issues two hundred and forty business licences a year through the same office. Applicants who wait in the ordinary queue receive approval in about eight months. Several members described a separate arrangement in which an unofficial sum, described as a facilitation payment, brings approval within a fortnight. Two applicants told us the sum was suggested by the clerk and that refusing it meant waiting out the full eight months. Nobody described the ordinary route as unreliable.

questions.stem: A traders' note on licensing is reproduced in the survey report below.

options.text: The queue described in the note is simply inefficient administration, since the ordinary route eventually issues licences
options.misconception: treats delay as the whole explanation

options.text: The note describes rent-seeking, because a discretionary permission creates a prize worth paying for quickly
The note describes tax collection, since the sums paid to the clerk fund the licensing service
options.misconception: reclassifies an unofficial fee as a lawful charge

options.text: The note describes theft, since the clerk keeps sums that belong to the district treasury
options.misconception: assumes the payments went to a public account

questions.explanation: Rent-seeking arises when a scarce permission is allocated by discretion, so its holder captures value by securing it early. An eight-month wait against a fortnight for a payment shows that prize.
questions.hint: Ask what the applicant buys with the payment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A licensing queue before and after reform
questions.learningObjective: Report both the gain and the unresolved element of a queue reform
questions.stem: A district governor asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, what a reform of the licensing queue achieved and what it left unresolved.

answer.exemplar: The reform shortened the typical wait sharply, with the median falling from 240 days to 75 days, so most applicants now receive a decision far sooner than before. It did not remove the queue. The published target is 60 days, the longest observed wait remained near 190 days, and payment for faster service was reported mostly by applicants who waited longest, which suggests that a fast route still exists for those able to pay. The reform therefore improved access for the ordinary applicant while leaving the discretionary element of the process intact.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate reports the reform's measured gain and the part it did not touch. A strong answer separates the improved typical case from the persistent tail and the reported fast route.
questions.hint: Compare the median, the target and the longest wait.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tenure and the defence of office
questions.learningObjective: Explain how protected tenure insulates an officeholder from removal
questions.stem: The survey finds that two thirds of district health officers hold posts protected by multi-year tenure.

options.text: Tenure is harmful because it allows competent officers to be dismissed without reason
options.misconception: assumes tenure means dismissal at will

options.text: Tenure is neutral, since officers with long terms are usually paid less than others
options.misconception: claims a pay offset the survey does not record

options.text: Tenure insulates officeholders, so their posts are defended even when performance is poor
Tenure weakens office because officers can refuse any instruction that they disagree with
options.misconception: assumes tenure directly causes refusal of orders

questions.explanation: Protected tenure raises the cost of removing an officeholder and adds perquisites to holding the post, so incumbents want to preserve it. Officers on probationary terms face none of those costs.
questions.hint: Ask what it costs to move a protected officer.

options.text: Since 45 appointments used examination, the process is largely merit based and nepotism is marginal
options.misconception: judges the system by the largest single category only

options.text: The figures show that internal candidates are favoured, because 21 of 90 posts went to serving officers
options.misconception: reads an internal share as proof of favouritism

options.text: Nepotism cannot be assessed here, since the survey did not record whether candidates were related
options.misconception: denies what the table states

options.text: Family appointments make up 27 per cent of all posts, and a further 23 per cent went to serving officers

questions.explanation: Twenty-four of 90 is about 27 per cent and 21 of 90 about 23, so family and insider appointments account for half of all posts. The examination route supplied the other half.
questions.hint: Convert each category into a share of the total.

questions.topic: Bribery incidence in a service survey
questions.learningObjective: State what a survey incidence figure can and cannot support
questions.stem: A survey team visits 200 households and asks whether they paid an unofficial fee for a clinic certificate in the past year; 46 say yes.

options.text: The figure is reported experience among those reached, and may understate prevalence where people stayed away
The figure is the true prevalence of bribery in the district, because 200 households is a large enough sample
options.misconception: assumes a large sample removes selection effects

options.text: The figure is the number of bribes paid in the district, since each respondent paid exactly one
options.misconception: converts a share into an event count

options.text: The figure is the share of clinic staff who demanded payment, since respondents all used the same clinic
options.misconception: reads household reports as staff behaviour

questions.explanation: A service survey measures what respondents say happened to them, for a named service and period. Sample size affects precision, not coverage, so non-response and self-report bias can shift the estimate.
questions.hint: Ask what the sample can and cannot cover.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Explain why recorded losses understate the harm done to the public purse
questions.stem: The survey report must advise the governor on why corruption losses do not show up in the district's published accounts.

options.text: Because the money is small and petty, so it is written off rather than recorded as an asset
options.misconception: explains the gap by size alone

options.text: Because the loss appears as an ordinary cost of the service, not as a line item named corruption
Because the district's books are kept by an outside agency that classifies items differently
options.misconception: invents an outside bookkeeper to explain the gap

options.text: Because the funds lost to corruption were borrowed rather than raised, so they never appear
options.misconception: assumes borrowed funds escape the budget entirely

questions.explanation: An unofficial fee or inflated invoice is booked as an ordinary payment, so the budget line looks spent while the public receives less. Accounts record transactions, not their fairness, so the loss leaves no trace of its own.
questions.hint: Ask how the payment appears on the budget line.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery as a cost of doing business
questions.learningObjective: Read reported bribes as a cost imposed on trading firms

stimulus.body: We surveyed 90 small traders about the cost of obtaining a trading licence and a market stall permit. Thirty-four said they had paid an unofficial sum in the last year, and the average amount was 900. Nine of them said they had put the cost into their prices, nineteen said they had absorbed it, and six said they had stopped renewing one of the permits. Several respondents asked us not to record which stalls they operate, saying the licence holder already knows their business.

questions.stem: The survey quotes a traders' association note; the note is reproduced below.

options.text: The note shows the payments are too small to matter, since most traders absorbed them without changing prices
options.misconception: dismisses small sums by how few traders pass them on

options.text: The note shows the payments are a legitimate fee, since the association collected them on the traders' behalf
options.misconception: assumes collection implies legality

options.text: The note shows the payments as a business cost, with some passed on and some deterring investment
The note shows the payments are rare, since fewer than half of the traders reported paying anything
options.misconception: reads the count as rarity without weighing the cost

questions.explanation: A payment required for a permit is an input cost whether passed on or not. Thirty-four traders paying 900 each is a predictable charge across 90 businesses, and six gave up a permit instead.
questions.hint: Ask how the payment changed trading decisions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Rent-seeking through a licence
questions.learningObjective: Explain the social cost of rent-seeking even when the licence is eventually issued
questions.stem: A policy adviser asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, why rent-seeking wastes resources even when the licence is eventually issued.

answer.exemplar: A licence confers the right to trade, and that right is what carries value. When officials can decide who obtains it quickly, the applicants compete for the officials' attention instead of competing to provide a better service, and resources are spent on cultivating connections, gifts and intermediaries. The licence itself is issued in due course, so the queue appears to move, but the effort of the applicants has gone into securing priority rather than into the activity the licence was meant to enable. Society gains nothing from that effort, and the informal payment itself does no work that the applicant did not pay for twice.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate explains the social cost of rent-seeking rather than only its shape. A strong answer shows how effort and money are diverted to priority rather than to the licensed activity.
questions.hint: Ask where the applicants' effort actually went.

questions.explanation: Cutting the median from 240 to 75 days is a large gain, and calling that a failure ignores how much changed. But 75 days still exceeds the 60-day standard, so progress is real and incomplete.

options.misconception: asserts a fixed visibility order without grounding it

options.text: Because only bribery is a criminal matter under the district's law

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Identify a loss to the public purse that is documented yet invisible in the accounts

stimulus.body: The appropriation for the district's outreach programme is 4,200,000 units, of which 3,900,000 is disbursed to contracted teams and 300,000 is held centrally for supervision and reporting. The supervision and reporting line has been used in each of the last three years to pay an additional allowance to the team leader in each of the twelve districts, described in the file as an honorarium for additional duty. The recipients are named. No line in the appropriation refers to corruption, and the payments were approved individually by the programme office.

questions.stem: The survey quotes an extract from a district budget paper; the extract is reproduced below.

options.text: The 300,000 is unaccounted for, because no explanation in the file covers payments of this kind

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery as a cost of doing business
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an unofficial payment from a lawful charge for a service
questions.stem: A business association asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, why bribery is best understood as a cost of doing business rather than as a tax.

answer.exemplar: A tax is a declared charge for a service the payer receives, set by law, publicly known and capable of appeal. An unofficial payment is none of those things: it is demanded informally, its size is not published, the payer cannot appeal it, and no service is attached to it, or only a service that was already owed. Because it enters the firm's accounts as an unavoidable operating expense, it raises the firm's costs, and those costs reach other traders and consumers through higher prices. Calling it a tax hides the part that matters, which is that no lawful charge stands behind it.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate distinguishes a lawful, published charge from an informal compulsory payment and links that to prices. A strong answer explains why the label matters for who bears the cost.
questions.hint: Ask what stands behind the payment.

questions.explanation: Rent-seeking consists of payments for an advantage in a discretionary process, such as faster access to a licence. What is bought is priority rather than a service, so cost is added without output.

questions.topic: Three forms of corruption
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bribery, theft and fraud are separable despite overlapping cases

stimulus.body: We asked 120 officials across three departments to describe a payment they had personally witnessed in the last year. Sixty-one described a sum handed to an official in exchange for a service the applicant was entitled to receive. Twenty-eight described public funds taken from a till or a store without authorisation. Thirty-one described a document signed that did not reflect what was supplied. In several accounts the same applicant both paid an official and received goods of the wrong specification, so the categories overlap in the events even though the mechanisms differ.

questions.stem: The survey cites a note on how officials move money; the note is reproduced below.

options.text: The three mechanisms are separable, since payment, taking and falsification are distinct even where one case shows two of them
The categories overlap so heavily that the three forms cannot be counted separately at all
options.misconception: lets overlap in cases dissolve the mechanisms

options.text: The forms are actually one, because each case shows an official exercising improper discretion
options.misconception: collapses the mechanisms into a single general category

options.text: The three forms are a property of the departments, since each department reported one mechanism only
options.misconception: attributes the mechanisms to departments rather than to acts

questions.explanation: Bribery, theft and fraud are defined by mechanism rather than by who is involved, so one case can show more than one. That overlap affects how cases are counted, not whether the mechanisms are distinguishable.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the harm to the public purse exceeds the sums paid to officials
questions.stem: A finance officer asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, why the cost of corruption to the public purse exceeds the value of the sums actually paid to officials.

answer.exemplar: The sums paid to officials are only the visible part. Each payment of 500 buys a service that the citizen was entitled to receive for nothing, so the public has paid twice: once through taxes and again through the fee. The payment also displaces activity, because the citizen spends time and money on the transaction rather than on the work the licence was meant to enable. At the institutional level, staff time spent negotiating and recording informal payments is not spent delivering services, and the queue it creates slows access for everyone, including those who never pay. These additional costs are why the harm to the public purse cannot be read off the amount handed over.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate identifies costs beyond the transferred sum, such as double payment, displaced activity and staff time. A strong answer shows why harm exceeds the counted amounts.
questions.hint: Ask what else the payment costs besides the sum.

options.misconception: keeps refusals in the denominator and hides the rate

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Three forms of corruption
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bribery, theft and fraud are treated as three separate forms
questions.stem: A teacher asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, why bribery, theft and fraud are treated as three forms of corruption rather than one.

answer.exemplar: They differ in the mechanism by which public resources are lost. In bribery a service or permission is sold to the applicant, so the loss is the value of the service plus whatever is paid for priority. In theft, funds are simply taken from a till, a store or a payroll without any service being delivered, so the loss is the amount taken. In fraud, a false document or an inflated price misdirects payment for something that was not delivered as described, so the loss is the difference between what was paid and what was received. Separating them matters because each leaves a different trail for auditors and calls for a different control.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate separates the forms by mechanism and connects that to detection. A strong answer explains what each form does to public resources rather than listing names.
questions.hint: Ask how each form takes the resource.

questions.topic: Rent-seeking through a licence
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total value of unofficial expedite fees paid by applicants
questions.stem: The survey finds that 250 applicants paid an unofficial expedite fee of 900 units to move a licence application through the office. What is the total value of those expedite fees?
questions.explanation: 250 applicants at 900 units each give 250 times 900, which is 225,000. The sum buys priority rather than a service, and most of those applicants would have received the licence eventually anyway.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of applicants by the fee.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A licensing queue before and after reform
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a queue can shrink on average yet still be experienced as unmanageable
questions.stem: The survey team must explain to the governor why a queue that shrank on average can still be experienced by applicants as unmanageable.

options.text: Because applicants often misremember how long they waited, so the survey figures overstate the improvement
options.misconception: dismisses measured waiting times in favour of memory

options.text: Because the reform moved the waiting around rather than reducing it in total
options.misconception: asserts a redistribution the data does not show

options.text: Because the distribution matters: a much shorter median can sit alongside waits that barely changed
Because the published standard was never communicated to the applicants who waited longest
options.misconception: explains experience by communication rather than by the distribution

questions.explanation: Waiting time is not only a median. If the longest waits fell less than the typical wait, applicants at the tail have gained little, and a queue measured by its middle value looks better than the queue they met.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the longest waits.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tenure and the defence of office
questions.learningObjective: Relate a difference in refusals to the cost each group bears for leaving office

stimulus.body: We compared 22 district officers whose posts carried fixed three-year terms with 22 whose posts could be ended on 60 days' notice. In the fixed-term group, 14 had declined a transfer offered by a superior in the previous two years; in the notice group, 3 had declined one. Asked why they declined, fixed-term officers referred to the pension and severance attached to their post and to the value of the local relationships they had built, while the notice group referred to the difficulty of settling their families in the posting. The two groups had similar seniority and similar workloads.

questions.stem: The survey quotes a note from a study of officeholding; the note is reproduced below.

options.text: The fixed-term officers refused more often because they were senior enough to be offered transfers
options.misconception: treats a shared feature of the two groups as the cause of the difference

options.text: The difference is explained by the workloads, since notice-period officers reported heavier duties
options.misconception: invents a workload difference the note rules out

options.text: The difference shows that notice-period officers are more obedient as a matter of training
options.misconception: assumes a training difference the note does not record

options.text: The difference fits the cost of losing office, which the notice group bears and the fixed-term group avoids

questions.explanation: Declining a transfer means giving up the post's benefits and continuity, and only one group carries that cost. The fixed-term group's reasons name severance and local ties, which is the defence tenure buys.
questions.hint: Ask what each group gives up by refusing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Nepotism in appointment
questions.learningObjective: Explain why nepotism is damaging even when the relatives appointed are competent
questions.stem: A governor asks the biologist to explain, for the survey report, why nepotism is damaging even when the relatives appointed are competent.

answer.exemplar: Nepotism is a statement about how posts are allocated, not about the quality of the person in the post. If relatives reach senior roles through family connection rather than open competition, the process no longer selects the most able candidate, so the average quality of the senior service falls even when this round's appointments happen to be good. It also closes off the routes by which people without family connections can reach the top, which discourages the ambitious from competing for public service, and it concentrates advantage in a way that the public can no longer check or contest through the appointment process itself.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate separates fairness of the selection process from the competence of the appointee. A strong answer shows why a good appointment reached the wrong way still causes harm.
questions.hint: Ask what the process selects besides a person.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery incidence in a service survey
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rise in reported incidence does not by itself establish a rise in payments demanded
questions.stem: A survey team's brief notes that the incidence of reported payments at clinics rose from 9 per cent to 17 per cent after a fee schedule was introduced.

options.text: The rise may reflect better recognition or willingness to report rather than more payments being demanded
The rise proves that introducing a fee schedule caused more corruption in the clinics
options.misconception: reads correlation as established causation

options.text: The rise proves nothing, because perception-based measures cannot track change of any kind
options.misconception: dismisses all change in a perception-based series

options.text: The rise shows the fee schedule was well designed, since clinics are now reporting more openly
options.misconception: reads a rise in reports as evidence of good design

questions.explanation: Reported incidence can move because practice changed or because people began reporting what they always faced. Without an independent measure, the survey flags a change but cannot attribute it to the fee schedule.
questions.hint: Ask what else could move a reported rate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Three forms of corruption
questions.learningObjective: Compare the shares of three corruption forms in a survey of incidents
questions.stem: A survey table classifies 210 observed incidents: 96 as bribery, 58 as theft of public funds and 56 as procurement fraud, with 12 incidents fitting more than one category.

options.text: Bribery accounts for the largest share of incidents, at about 46 per cent of the 210 observed
options.misconception: ignores the twelve incidents classified twice

options.text: Each category covers a substantial share of the incidents, so no single mechanism dominates the district's cases
Procurement fraud is marginal at 27 per cent, since the other two categories are larger
options.misconception: calls a substantial share marginal without a threshold

options.text: The categories cannot overlap, because a payment and a false invoice are different events by definition
options.misconception: denies the overlap the table records

questions.explanation: 96 of 210 is about 46 per cent, 58 about 28 and 56 about 27, so bribery leads without dominating. That matters for the response: three substantial mechanisms need controls aimed at each, not one.
questions.hint: Convert each category into a share and compare.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of corruption to the public purse
questions.learningObjective: Identify the public cost hidden inside a donation followed by an award
questions.stem: A survey respondent explains that a clinic accepted a donated water tank, and that the donor was later given the only contract for fitting pumps.

options.text: The arrangement is neutral, because the tank was donated freely to the clinic
options.misconception: ignores the consideration given for the donation

options.text: The arrangement harms the clinic, because the donated tank was of a lower standard than planned
options.misconception: assumes a quality claim the respondent did not make

options.text: The arrangement costs the public, because the contract was steered rather than competed for
The arrangement is beneficial, because donations let the district build more than its budget allows
options.misconception: ignores the price paid for the donation

questions.explanation: A donation followed by the award of the only contract is not an ordinary gift, since the consideration was provided through the contract. The district pays the usual price and gets less competition.
questions.hint: Ask what consideration changed hands.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Bribery as a cost of doing business
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the combined unofficial payment across a sample of trading firms
questions.stem: The survey finds that 50 sampled firms each with turnover of 120,000 units spend 6 per cent of turnover on unofficial payments. What is the combined unofficial payment across the sample?
questions.explanation: Each firm pays 6 per cent of 120,000, which is 7,200, and across 50 firms that is 360,000. On the sample's turnover of 6,000,000 units, that is the cost firms without connections must absorb.
questions.hint: Take the percentage of turnover for each firm, then add.
